title: Queueing systems
subtitle: Waiting is what most systems are made of. A few formulas tell you when the line explodes.

sections.title: Elements of a queue
sections.body: A queueing system has an arrival process (calling population, inter-arrival times), a queue (capacity, discipline — FIFO, LIFO, priority) and one or more servers (service-time distribution). Kendall’s notation A/B/c/K/N/D describes it: M/M/1 = Markovian (Poisson) arrivals, Markovian (exponential) service, one server. Applications: banks, call centres, routers, CPUs, traffic.

questions.prompt: In M/M/1 the second “M” stands for…

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The first M is Poisson arrivals.

figures.caption: Figure 4.1.1 — a single-server queue
figures.note: The anatomy of an M/M/1 queue.

sections.title: M/M/1 in theory
sections.body: With arrival rate λ and service rate μ the utilisation is ρ = λ/μ, which must stay below 1. Then L (mean number in system) = ρ/(1−ρ), W (mean time in system) = 1/(μ−λ), Lq = ρ²/(1−ρ), Wq = ρ/(μ−λ), and Little’s law L = λW holds for any stable queue. At ρ = 0.5: L = 1. At ρ = 0.9: L = 9 — waiting explodes as utilisation approaches 100%.

worked.why: Mean time in system, and Little’s law check L = λW.

questions.prompt: What happens to an M/M/1 queue as ρ → 1?

choices.text: The mean queue length and waiting time grow without bound.

sections.title: Simulating it
sections.body: Generate exponential inter-arrival and service times, run the event loop, and measure. With λ = 0.5, μ = 1 (ρ = 0.5) over 4000 customers the simulated utilisation is 0.512 and average number in system 1.012 against theory ρ = 0.5, L = 1. At ρ = 0.9 the theory says L = 9 and the simulation gives about 11.148 — with much more noise.

questions.prompt: Why is the ρ = 0.9 simulation noisier than ρ = 0.5?

choices.text: Long busy periods make the queue correlated over time, so averages converge slowly.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: More runs or longer runs are needed.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: Theory is fine; estimating it is harder.

figures.caption: Figure 4.3.1 — ρ = 0.5
figures.note: Steps show the queue length over time; ticks are arrivals and departures.

figures.caption: Figure 4.3.2 — ρ = 0.9
figures.note: Near saturation the queue wanders to large values.

problems.prompt: λ = 0.5, μ = 1: give the theoretical utilisation, L and mean wait in queue, and compare with the simulation.
problems.answer: ρ = 0.5, L = 1, Wq = ρ/(μ−λ) = 1. Simulated: utilisation 0.512, L ≈ 1.012.

sections.title: Networks of queues
sections.body: Real systems chain queues: a customer visits several stations. In a tandem of M/M/1 queues, each behaves (Jackson's theorem) as an independent M/M/1 with the same arrival rate but its own μ, and the total time is the sum. More servers (M/M/c) share the load: the same λ with two half-speed servers behaves differently from one full-speed server.

worked.why: Two M/M/1 stations in series, λ = 2/min, μ₁ = 4, μ₂ = 3.

questions.prompt: In a tandem of two queues the total time in the system is…

choices.text: The sum of the times at each station.

sections.title: Applications
sections.body: Sizing a call-centre (how many agents keep waiting under 30 s), router buffers, CPU scheduling, hospital beds, checkout lanes. The simulator shows the danger zone: keep utilisation below about 70–80% if waiting matters.

questions.prompt: Why do real systems avoid 100% utilisation?

choices.text: Queues and delays grow without bound as ρ approaches 1.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Some idle capacity buys short waits.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
• ρ = λ/μ < 1; L = ρ/(1−ρ); W = 1/(μ−λ); L = λW.
  • Simulation agrees with theory, with noise growing near ρ = 1.
